keywords: Why toast lands butter side down: Murphy's law, the table edge, rotation, Robert Matthews toast experiment. Physics simulation.
description: Does toast really land butter side down, or is it just Murphy's law? We test three cases on the same slice: pushed slowly off a kitchen table (75 cm), flicked off fast, then pushed slowly off a 3 m table.
From the kitchen table the toast lands butter side down. Flicked off fast, it barely spins and lands butter side up. From a 3 m table it has time for a full turn and lands butter side up.

Why: a slice pushed slowly off a table first tips over the edge, pivoting on it. That pivot sets it spinning, but slowly. From an ordinary table it only has time for about half a turn before it hits the floor, so the butter ends up underneath. Physicist Robert Matthews showed in 1995 that a table would have to be about 3 metres high to give the toast time to come back butter side up; pushed off faster than about 1.6 m/s, it leaves the edge before it can tip.
It is not just theory: in 2001, more than 1,000 schoolchildren dropped toast over 21,000 times, and it landed butter side down 62% of the time (The Telegraph, 27 May 2001).
This video is a 3D simulation (Blender) of Matthews' model; the motion is simulated.
sources_detail: R. A. J. Matthews, 'Tumbling toast, Murphy's Law and the fundamental constants', European Journal of Physics 16, 172 (1995), doi:10.1088/0143-0807/16/4/005: toast has an inherent tendency to land butter side down for a wide range of conditions; for conventional tables (h about 75 cm) it lacks the rotation to land butter up; a table about 3 m high would be needed; tumbling is negligible for horizontal speeds above about 1.6 m/s.

The Telegraph (Robert Matthews), 27 May 2001: nationwide experiment, more than 1,000 schoolchildren, toast tumbling off plates more than 21,000 times, butter side down 62 per cent of the time. Also BBC Science Focus: 'over 1,000 schoolchildren and 21,000 drops', butter side down almost two thirds of the time.

On screen: 75 cm, 3 m and 1.6 m/s from Matthews 1995; 21,000 drops and 62% from the 2001 experiment. Simulated: the slice (12 cm), the push, the pivot and the fall follow Matthews' model (pivot on the edge, then constant spin); the spin dial shows the simulated angle, no number.
